question: Why are activist discount-arbitrage investors reluctant to target digital asset treasury companies trading at steep discounts to NAV, even though they actively target discounted closed-end funds?
guest: One of the issues for us with digital asset treasury companies, which we don't have with closed-end funds or BDCs, is that as an activist you are always worried they are going to do something really dilutive, effectively a poison pill. I don't believe it is impossible for a digital asset treasury company to issue shares way below NAV, maybe even well below the price it is trading at, to a select group of investors. If they issued it to everyone, you'd say, "Okay, I can get my pro rata portion." But I would hate to buy something at a 35% discount to NAV and find that they issue a lot of shares at 50 to a select group, and now I've been diluted. Because it is not a '40 Act closed-end fund—closed-end funds cannot do dilutive offerings without offering them to everyone. And the second thing is a digital asset treasury company can decide it wants to pay its CEO a lot of money and have a handpicked board and basically take money out that way.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Activists target discounted closed-end funds because the regulatory structure gives them a reliable path to closing the gap: funds registered under the Investment Company Act have independent boards, annual director elections, leverage limits, and well-trodden mechanisms (tender offers, open-ending, liquidation) that force value toward NAV. Digital asset treasury companies (DATs) lack most of that, so the discount is far harder to capture.

DATs are operating companies, not registered funds, so no rule obliges them to redeem or liquidate at NAV. Many have entrenched control: founder or sponsor blocks, staggered boards, dual-class shares, and management or asset-management agreements with costly termination fees. Their balance sheets also complicate the arithmetic, since convertible debt, preferred stock, warrants, and PIPE shares awaiting registration mean the headline "mNAV" overstates what common holders would actually receive. Tokens may be locked, staked, or illiquid, so selling them to fund buybacks would depress the very NAV being pursued.

Finally, the trade is hard to hedge and expensive to run: crypto volatility, costly stock borrow, tax leakage on liquidation, and small floats make a contested campaign unattractive relative to the potential payoff.

This is from general knowledge, not a fresh search.

models.answer:
Closed-end funds (CEFs) are governed by the Investment Company Act of 1940, which protects arbitrageurs pushing for tender offers, buybacks, or liquidation. Crucially, the 1940 Act generally bars CEFs from issuing shares below net asset value (NAV), caps leverage, restricts self-dealing, and subjects fees and custodianship to strict fiduciary oversight, keeping per-share NAV intact during a proxy contest.

Digital asset treasury companies (DATs), by contrast, are operating corporations outside those statutory guardrails. Even when activists hedge the underlying crypto price, DAT boards and insiders can erode per-share NAV before the discount closes by issuing dilutive equity below NAV, awarding excessive executive pay, funding unprofitable operations, or making value-destructive acquisitions. DATs also wield potent corporate defenses, including dual-class voting stock, poison pills, staggered boards, and strict advance-notice bylaws, alongside complex convertible debt and potential corporate taxes upon liquidating appreciated tokens. Because governance abuse and unchecked dilution can drain per-share backing, the discount cannot be reliably arbitraged.

noweb.answer:
Activist arbitrageurs rely on predictable legal, tax, and hedging mechanics in closed-end funds (CEFs) that largely vanish in digital asset treasury companies (DATs). Regulated under the Investment Company Act of 1940, CEFs feature independent boards, strict leverage limits, and pass-through tax status, giving activists established pathways to force tender offers, liquidations, or open-end conversions near full net asset value.

By contrast, DATs are operating corporations shielded by the business judgment rule and frequently insulated by dual-class shares, insider voting control, staggered boards, or poison pills that neutralize hostile proxy campaigns. Even when governance hurdles are surmountable, realizable liquidation value is eroded by corporate-level taxes on appreciated crypto, legacy operating cash burn, management severance, ongoing share dilution, and complex senior claims such as convertible notes or preferred stock. Finally, discount arbitrage requires shorting the underlying asset while campaigning for a catalyst, and crypto’s extreme volatility, funding rates, margin squeeze risk, and staking lockups make maintaining a delta-neutral hedge far costlier and riskier over a protracted fight than hedging traditional CEF portfolios.

Selling the coins could trigger corporate tax, and management can keep issuing shares or buying more crypto, which moves the target. The discount itself is volatile because crypto prices swing so much, which makes long campaigns expensive. Shareholder activism at these companies is rising, but these obstacles make the closed-end fund playbook hard to repeat.

Activists like Saba profit from closed-end fund discounts because the playbook is reliable. The funds hold liquid, transparently priced securities, sit under the 1940 Act's governance framework, and can be pushed through proxy fights into tender offers, open-ending or liquidation that hands shareholders close to NAV. The discount is a fairly hedgeable, mean-reverting spread.

Digital asset treasury companies lack most of those levers. They are ordinary operating companies, often founder-controlled through super-voting shares, insider-heavy or staggered boards, and sometimes poison pills, so a proxy campaign has little chance. Many are financed with convertible notes and preferred stock that rank ahead of common equity, so a forced wind-down sends much of the "NAV" to creditors first. Liquidating large token positions could trigger taxes, move thin markets, and run into lockups or custody frictions. The NAV itself is volatile, so the activist must either hold unhedged crypto exposure or pay to short tokens. Some companies also mix in operating businesses or external-manager arrangements that blur the true liquidation value. Together these make the discount less a capturable arbitrage than a risky, contested bet.

Activist discount-arbitrage investors rely heavily on the structural guardrails of the Investment Company Act of 1940, which govern closed-end funds but do not apply to digital asset treasury companies (DATs). Under the 1940 Act, closed-end funds generally cannot issue new shares below net asset value without shareholder approval, face strict limits on leverage, self-dealing, and takeover defenses, and hold transparent portfolios that activists can hedge while pushing for tender offers or liquidation.

By contrast, DATs are structured as ordinary operating corporations. Without 1940 Act protections, entrenched managers can destroy the arbitrage by issuing dilutive shares below NAV, paying themselves excessive executive compensation or advisory fees, adopting poison pills or dual-class voting structures, or diverting capital into unrelated operating businesses. Moreover, DATs face corporate-level tax liabilities if forced to liquidate appreciated crypto holdings, and their extreme underlying volatility makes hedging during a protracted proxy fight costly and unreliable. Consequently, a steep discount to NAV in a DAT often reflects genuine governance and dilution risk rather than a clean, capturable mispricing.

Digital asset treasury companies, by contrast, are operating corporations that lack these structural protections. Founders and insiders often hold super-voting stock, staggered boards, or poison pills, while corporate directors enjoy wide business-judgment discretion to resist liquidation. Even when an activist gains influence, unlocking NAV is severely impaired by corporate tax leakage on appreciated crypto holdings, complex capital stacks of convertible debt and preferred stock, and illiquid or locked token positions. Finally, hedging the underlying exposure is far harder: extreme crypto volatility, high borrow or funding costs, and margin risk make a long-equity, short-token arbitrage trade dangerous to carry through a protracted proxy fight before any catalyst materializes.

noweb.answer:
A steep discount matters to an arbitrageur only if there’s a credible way to turn it into cash. Closed-end funds have a familiar playbook. Activists can rally shareholders to press for a tender offer near NAV, liquidation, or conversion to an open-end fund that allows redemptions.

Digital asset treasury companies are corporations, and shareholders generally have no right to redeem their shares for the underlying coins. Founders or insiders may control enough votes to block a sale or distribution, and management may prefer to keep accumulating crypto. The headline discount can also overstate the payoff if the reported NAV omits debt, taxes, or dilution. Even where the crypto exposure can be hedged, that hedge cannot make the board return capital. Without a realistic path to a payout, the discount can persist or widen.

Buying shares at a discount to net asset value (NAV) only pays off if the discount closes or the investor can get the company to distribute the assets. Closed-end fund activists have familiar ways to do that, such as pressing for a tender offer near NAV or a vote to convert the fund to an open-end structure. A digital asset treasury company is an operating corporation. Its shareholders have no right to redeem their shares for crypto, and insiders may control enough votes to block a sale or liquidation.

That leaves an activist facing a potentially long proxy fight while the crypto holdings fluctuate in value. Debt, preferred claims, and taxes on a sale can also reduce what common shareholders would actually receive. The headline discount can therefore look much larger than the profit an activist can realistically capture.
